items.title: 67559_Art Hodes oral history interview
items.q: we were kids at Hull House, and his bandmaster brought him in to where I was playing for the dancers. And he asked me if I minded if the kid played with me.

ctx.x: Everybody got very excited, and I said, what's all the excitement about? Benny Goodman. So, who's Benny Goodman? He's got a big band. I wasn't interested. I was interested in small bands, even then. He came with John Hammond and he came with this girl singer and I think at that time it was Helen Forrest.

And everybody -- the King was here, the whole place they're running to his table. I didn't run to his table, because I remember him as a kid. See, we were kids at Hull House, and his bandmaster brought him in to where I was playing for the dancers. And he asked me if I minded if the kid played with me. And I looked at this kid, with a head that seemed so outsized and even though the head was outsized, the ego was outsized, too. And he had such an assurance, and just a tilt of the nose, almost.
About how old was he then?

items.title: 67559_Art Hodes oral history interview
items.q: And I loved Duke, I collected Duke. But I didn't think he needed my help

ctx.x: Leonard Feather, the critic, and I fell apart. Because he came up to that station with Duke Ellington records. And I had a very narrow -- as honestly as I can be now -- approach to what I thought my role of promoting jazz was. I say narrow from the standpoint of where I sit now. It wasn't bad, I believed in it, I believe in it now. But it was very close. It had to be the Hot Five's, the Hot Seven's, Bessie Smith, James P. Johnson, Fats Waller -- that era of jazz.
And I loved Duke, I collected Duke. But I didn't think he needed my help, and I think that music did.
